Welcome toDividing the Energy

Two systems share a fixed energy across a wall — how does it divide?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: how two systems in thermal contact divide a fixed energy

Source

Concept
Two systems of N₁ and N₂ particles are separated by a rigid wall that passes energy but no particles; the pair is isolated, so U = U₁ + U₂ is fixed. With Ω₁ ∝ U₁^(αN₁), Ω₂ ∝ U₂^(αN₂) and α = 1, a division of the energy is found with probability proportional to Ω₁(U₁)Ω₂(U − U₁). The peak sits where ∂(ln Ω₁)/∂U₁ = ∂(ln Ω₂)/∂U₂, the statistical condition for equal temperature (1/T = kB ∂ln Ω/∂U).
On screen
Top: Ω₁Ω₂ divided by its peak value against U₁/U₁*, where U₁* is the most probable energy of system 1; the blue arrow marks the Gaussian width ΔU₁ at height e^(−1/2). Bottom: U₁/U₁* and U₂/U₂* for the last 200 looks, ten per second; each look is an independent, exact draw of the division. The Readouts panel in the sidebar gives ΔU₁/U₁* and ΔU₂/U₂* to three significant figures, and how far the latest look strays from the most probable division, U₁/U₁* − 1 and U₂/U₂* − 1.
Serves
The course objective on how the spread of the energy division depends on the sizes N₁ and N₂ of the two systems.
Inquiry
Five question cards, then a closing summary; each card sets the sizes it asks about, and N₁ and N₂ change one decade at a time.
Misconception
Each card's choices probe a common intuition about equilibrium, exchange across the wall and system size; feedback appears once a choice is made.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit, then checkFive gated question cards; on each card the width and latest-look readouts show an em dash until a choice is committed.
Operational quantitiesΔU₁/U₁* and ΔU₂/U₂* are given to three significant figures and can be read against the blue ΔU₁ arrow on the plot; the latest-look strays show the exchange going on even when the traces are flat.
Exact modelThe curve is ln f(y) = αN₁ ln y + αN₂ ln(1 + (N₁/N₂)(1 − y)) with α = 1; every look is an exact draw of U₁/U from the beta distribution with parameters αN₁ + 1 and αN₂ + 1, made as G₁/(G₁ + G₂) from two gamma numbers.
Stable axesFixed ranges (0–2 in units of U₁*, 0–1.1 in units of the peak height, 0–2 in U/U*); nothing rescales when N₁ or N₂ changes.
Honest limitsA peak narrower than one pixel is drawn as a line at least one pixel thick, and the ΔU₁ arrow then puts its heads outside, pointing inwards. The arrow marks the Gaussian width 1 ± ΔU₁/U₁*; when N₁ ≪ N₂ the exact curve is lopsided, so its heads sit off the curve (at N₁ = 10, N₂ = 10⁶ the curve crosses e^(−1/2) at 0.716 and 1.350, not at 1 ± 0.316).
Independent looksLooks are independent, ten per second, so the strip shows how far the division strays, not how fast energy moves.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two small systems

Set N₁ = N₂ = 10 and press ▶ Play. Watch the thick U₁/U₁* trace in the lower strip, which shows the energy of the first system at each look as a fraction of its most probable value. What does the trace do?

2 · Growing both systems

Raise N₁ and N₂ together from 10 to 1000, keeping them equal. By about what factor does the width of the peak shrink?

3 · Very large systems

Set N₁ = N₂ = 10⁶. The peak is now a single vertical line and both traces lie flat on 1. Is energy still crossing the wall between the two systems?

4 · Growing only one system

Set N₁ = N₂ = 10 again, and then raise N₂ one decade at a time up to 10⁶, keeping N₁ at 10. What happens to the width of the peak?

5 · The small one keeps wandering

Keep N₁ = 10 and N₂ = 10⁶ and compare the two traces. Why does the thin orange U₂/U₂* trace of the large system lie flat while the thick U₁/U₁* trace of the small one wanders?

6 · Why large systems look steady

The division of the energy is spread over a peak of relative width ΔU₁/U₁* = √(N₂/(αN₁(N₁ + N₂))). For two equal systems that is √(1/(2αN)): 0.224 at N = 10, 7 × 10⁻⁴ at N = 10⁶, and about 10⁻¹² for a mole.

So in a macroscopic body the most probable division is, for all practical purposes, the only one ever seen, even though energy never stops crossing the wall. A small system in contact with a large one keeps its own spread, about 1/√(αN₁), however big its partner.

The Physics

Two Systems Dividing Their Energy · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two systems of N1 and N2 particles touch through a rigid wall that passes energy but no particles. The pair is isolated, so its total energy U is fixed. This sim shows how that energy is divided between the two systems, and how the division depends on their sizes.

What you'll learn

  • How the number of microstates of the pair depends on the division of the energy.
  • Where the most probable division sits.
  • How the width of the peak depends on N1 and N2.
  • Why a large system can look steady while energy still crosses the wall.
The set-up, after Figure 27 of the notes.

What's on screen

  • Upper plot: Ω1Ω2 divided by its peak value, against U1/U1*, where U1* is the most probable energy of system 1. A blue arrow marks the width ΔU1, and a dot on the axis marks the latest look.
  • Lower strip: U1/U1* as a thick dark trace and U2/U2* as a thin orange one, for the last 200 looks, ten per second.
  • Readouts: the widths ΔU1/U1* and ΔU2/U2*, and how far the latest look strays from the peak.
See itLook at the sim at your current settings, running. Watch for: the hump in the upper plot, and the two traces starting to fill the strip from the right.

Fixed: the multiplicities are Ω ∝ UαN with α = 1. The curve is exact, and each look is an independent, exact draw of the division, so the strip shows how far the division strays, not how fast energy moves.

03

The most probable division shares the energy in proportion to the sizes

Only energy crosses the wall, so the one free variable is U1, with U2 = U − U1. Every microstate of the pair is equally likely, so a division has a probability proportional to Ω1(U1)Ω2(U − U1), (4.20). With Ω ∝ UαN this is a hump.

ln Ωtot = αN1 ln U1 + αN2 ln (U − U1) + const
Notes, (4.21). Setting its derivative to zero gives αN1/U1 = αN2/U2.

The top of the hump is at U1* = U N1/(N1 + N2), so the energy is shared in proportion to the sizes. The plot's axis is U1 in units of U1*, so the peak always sits at 1, and the curve is scaled to 1 there.

The weight of every division for two systems of 10 particles.
See itSet N1 = N2 = 10 and press Play. Watch for: one hump with its top on the dashed line at U1/U1* = 1, falling to zero at 0 and at 2.
04

The curvature at the top sets the width of the peak

The second derivative at the top is −αN1/U1*2 − αN2/U2*2, (4.22). Expanding to second order makes Ωtot a Gaussian whose width ΔU1 is of order U/√N, (4.23)–(4.24). In the sim's units the fractional width is

ΔU1/U1* = √( N2 / (αN1(N1 + N2)) )
ΔU2/U2* is the same with N1 and N2 swapped. For equal sizes both are √(1/(2αN)).
The blue arrow is the width: 1 ± 0.224, at height e−1/2 of the peak.
See itSet N1 = N2 = 10 and press Play. Watch for: ΔU1/U1* = 0.224, and the blue arrow running from 0.776 to 1.224.
05

The width falls as the square root of N, not as N

For two equal systems, ΔU1/U1* = √(1/(2αN)). Raising N from 10 to 1000 is a hundredfold rise, so the width falls by √100 = 10, from 0.224 to 0.0224. Each step of the slider is a factor 10 in N, and a factor √10 = 3.16 in width. This is the 1/√N of (4.24): the peak narrows far more slowly than the systems grow.

The sim's six slider steps for equal systems: six decades of N, three of width.
See itSet N1 = N2 = 1000 and press Play. Watch for: ΔU1/U1* = 0.0224, and a blue arrow one tenth as long as at N = 10.
06

At a million particles each, the peak is a line but energy still crosses the wall

At N1 = N2 = 106, ΔU1/U1* = 7.07×10−4. That is narrower than a pixel on the plot, so the sim draws the peak as a vertical line, and both traces lie on 1.

The same plot at N = 10 and at N = 106.

Each look is a fresh draw of the division, so energy keeps crossing the wall in both directions. The division strays from U1* by about 7 parts in 104, too little to draw. The notes' point is the same: for a few particles the fluctuations are visible, for 1023 they are not.

See itSet N1 = N2 = 106 and press Play. Watch for: the peak as a line, flat traces, and U1/U1* − 1 in the readouts still changing from look to look.
07

A small system touching a large one keeps its own width

Keep N1 = 10 and raise N2. The width ΔU1/U1* rises from 0.224 and stops at 0.316, since for N2 ≫ N1 it tends to √(1/(αN1)), the width of system 1 alone. The large system's ΔU2/U2* keeps falling.

N2ΔU1/U1*ΔU2/U2*
100.2240.224
1000.3020.0302
10000.3153.15×10−3
1060.3163.16×10−6

U1 + U2 is fixed, so system 2 loses exactly what system 1 gains. But system 1 holds only U1*/U = N1/(N1 + N2) = 1.0×10−5 of the energy, so its swing is a few parts in 106 of system 2's store.

See itSet N1 = 10 and N2 = 106 and press Play. Watch for: the thick trace wandering while the thin orange one lies flat on 1.
08

Where it matters

  • Equal temperatures. The condition for the peak, ∂ln Ω1/∂U1 = ∂ln Ω2/∂U2, becomes 1/T1 = 1/T2 once S = kB ln Ω defines T (notes, (4.25)–(4.28)).
  • Macroscopic bodies. The same formula gives 9.1×10−13 for N = 6.02×1023 each, so no experiment could detect a departure from the most probable division.
  • The second law. Nothing forbids the entropy of an isolated system from falling; departures from the peak are of relative size 1/√N, overwhelmingly unlikely for a large system (notes, Section 4.2).
  • A system in a bath. A small system against a much larger one still swings by √(1/(αN1)). The large one fixes the temperature, not the small one's energy (the Boltzmann factor, Section 4.4).
Go deeper: the Gaussian is an approximation

The curve in the sim is exact; the Gaussian is only its expansion about the top. At N = 10 the exact curve at 1 ± 0.224 stands at 0.599 of the peak, against e−1/2 = 0.607, and at 1 ± 0.447 at 0.107 against 0.135. By N = 1000 the two agree to within 0.02% at one width. When N1 ≪ N2 the exact curve is also lopsided: at N1 = 10, N2 = 106 it crosses e−1/2 at 0.716 and 1.350, not at 1 ± 0.316, so the blue ΔU1 arrow, which marks the Gaussian width, reaches past the curve on the left and stops short of it on the right.

09

Summary

In one line. How tightly the energy of a pair of systems in contact sticks to its most probable division depends on the sizes N1 and N2 of the two systems, and the sim lets you set both.

Key points

  • The top of Ω1Ω2 is at U1* = U N1/(N1 + N2).
  • The fractional width is √(N2/(αN1(N1 + N2))): 0.224 at N = 10 each, falling as 1/√N.
  • Against a much larger system, a small one keeps ΔU1/U1* = 0.316.

Common mix-ups

  • “A hundredfold rise in N narrows the peak a hundredfold.” It narrows it tenfold: 0.224 to 0.0224.
  • “At 106 particles the energy has stopped moving.” The division still changes at every look, by about 7×10−4 of U1*.
  • “A huge neighbour makes a small system steady.” At N1 = 10 against 106 the width is still 0.316.

Things to try on your own

  • Step N1 = N2 from 10 to 106 and read the width at each step.
  • Keep N1 = 10 and raise N2. Where does ΔU1/U1* stop changing?
  • Try N1 = 106 and N2 = 10. Which trace wanders now?
